Comparison of SZ-HRX and LEHR collimators 
for reduced-duration 123I-ioflupane brain 
SPECT/CT: a phantom study
Mathieu Pavoine1, Kouider-Othmane Kelatma1, Clémence Robert1, Alexandre Rintaud1, Samuel Guigo1, 
Thomas Godefroy1, Pierre-Yves Salaün1,2,3, Solène Querellou1,2,3 and David Bourhis1,3*
EJNMMI Physics
Abstract
Background  123I-ioflupane Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography with 
Computed Tomography (SPECT-CT) imaging is widely used to assess dopaminergic 
denervation in parkinsonian syndromes, such as Parkinson’s disease and atypical 
variants. Standard imaging generally uses low-energy high-resolution (LEHR) parallel-
hole collimators, which require long acquisition times and minimal source-to-detector 
distance to optimize spatial resolution. Recently, the Smart-Zoom High-Resolution 
and eXtended magnification volume (SZ-HRX) solution was designed specifically 
for neurological applications. It incorporates multifocal collimators and a dedicated 
reconstruction algorithm, promising a reduction in acquisition duration, and an 
improvement in patient comfort by allowing detectors to be positioned further away 
from the head. The aim of this study is to investigate the performance of SZ-HRX 
system compared to LEHR collimators.
Methods  A striatal phantom with 5 compartments (putamens, caudates, and 
background) was filled with different concentrations of 123I-ioflupane to simulate 
various clinical situations. Tomographic acquisitions were performed on each LEHR and 
SZ-HRX system. The summation of dynamically acquired projections allowed testing 
different acquisition durations with the SZ-HRX collimator. Sensitivity and Spatial 
resolution were assessed and compared. The data were reconstructed according 
to EANM recommendations. Contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), striatum-to-background 
ratio (SBR), coefficient of variation (CV), and normalized asymmetry index (NAI) were 
calculated for both systems and compared to the LEHR acquisition. To estimate the 
shortest SZ-HRX acquisition duration, a linear regression of all quantitative results were 
calculated between the two systems.
Results  SZ-HRX collimation had superior performance characteristics than LEHR, with 
relative changes in CNR, CV, and SBR of + 99%, -28% and + 42% respectively, without 
any decrease in spatial resolution or change in asymmetry index. SZ-HRX system seems 
to be at least as good as LEHR system, up to 40% of scan time reduction.

Background
Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography with Computed Tomography (SPECT-
CT) imaging using 123I-ioflupane is widely used in the in vivo assessment of parkinsonian 
syndromes [1–4]. 123I-ioflupane binds selectively to striatal pre-synaptic dopaminergic 
receptors allowing analysis of nigrostriatal dopaminergic denervation. Striatal dopa­
minergic denervation can be found in idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, but also in atypi­
cal Parkinsonian syndromes, including Lewy body dementia, progressive supranuclear 
palsy, cortico-basal dementia and multi-system atrophy [1, 5]. It can therefore be used to 
differentiate parkinsonian disorders with and without dopaminergic denervation (essen­
tial tremor and iatrogenic parkinsonian syndromes), in patients with an unusual history 
or clinical picture, or a poor response to levodopa treatment [6–10].
This imaging test can be performed with several parallel collimators, such as Low-
Energy, High- (or Ultra-High) Resolution parallel-hole collimators (LEHR or LEUHR), 
Low-Energy Low Penetration (LELP), medium energy (ME), or dedicated brain sys­
tems, such as fan beam or multi pinhole collimators [11]. Striatal SPECT requires at 
least 1.5 million counts, resulting in a long acquisition duration for LEHR systems (20 
to 40  min according to the amount of administrated 123I-ioflupane). Moreover, rota­
tional radius must be as small as possible, because the spatial resolution depends on 
the source-detector distance. These two parameters (acquisition duration and distance 
between detectors and head) can be limiting, especially for patients with severe trem­
ors or claustrophobia [12]. In contrast, because they focus on the patient’s head, fan-
beam collimators can offer better comfort because they allow a larger radius and shorter 
acquisitions.
The use of non-conventional geometry collimators is already widely used in cardiol­
ogy [13–15]. Fan-beam collimation geometry centered on the heart, offers 3 to 4 times 
higher sensitivity compared with LEHR collimators, with no significant impact on other 
detection performances [16–18]. This significant improvement in sensitivity enables 
about 50% shorter acquisition duration, or a reduction of around 37.5% in effective dose, 
while maintaining comparable performances [19, 20]. The use of non parallel-hole col­
limators has also been investigated in neurology [21–24]. A study carried out on striatal 
phantoms in 2017 indicated that the use of a cardiac dedicated Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride 
(CZT) gamma camera, equipped with multi pinhole collimators, provided 2 to 3 times 
higher quantification on striatal 123I-ioflupane uptake, enabling shorter imaging times 
and/or a lower injected dose [25]. It should be noted that this improvement is probably 
due both to the difference in detection geometry and in detector type. Another study, 
designed to create a reference database for ultra-high-resolution fan-beam collimators, 
showed a significant improvement in Specific Binding Ratio (SBR) compared with par­
allel-hole collimators, with a particular 1.2 times higher SBR on striatal phantoms [26].
Smart-Zoom High Resolution and eXtended magnification volume (SZ-HRX) pack­
age has recently been released by Siemens Healthcare (Erlangen, Germany). SZ-HRX is 
Conclusion  SZ-HRX collimation showed superior performance characteristics to 
LEHR collimation in the study of 123I-ioflupane filled striatal phantom, enabling shorter 
acquisitions.

a specific multifocal fanbeam collimator designed for neurology. SMARTZOOM HRX 
differs from the cardiac SMARTZOOM collimator by utilizing smaller 1.5-mm hexago­
nal hole diameter and adapted focal lengths to accommodate a larger and more homog­
enous area of interest. A dedicated reconstruction algorithm has been developed to 
account for the geometry of the collimator in the reconstruction [27]. It promises a 20% 
reduction in acquisition duration compared to LEHR for neuroimaging with 99mTc and 
an improvement of patient comfort (the detectors being located further away), without 
reducing the examination quality [28].
The SZ-HRX collimation has recently been evaluated on phantoms, in both 99mTech­
netium (99mTc) and 123I-ioflupane [29, 30]. This system showed equivalent image quality 
for 99mTc, and higher image quality for 123I-ioflupane, compared with LEHR collimators. 
However, these two studies used a Hoffman phantom, which simulates cerebral perfu­
sion (by simulating cerebral cortex and basal ganglia uptake), rather than a striatal phan­
tom, which corresponds more closely to in vivo 123I-ioflupane uptake.
The aim of our study is therefore to investigate the performance of SZ-HRX system 
compared to parallel-hole collimators for 123I-ioflupane SPECT-CT, using a striatal 
phantom, then to consider the optimization opportunities in terms of acquisition dura­
tion for SZ-HRX system.
Materials and methods
Experimentations on phantoms
An anthropomorphic striatal phantom Alderson RSD (Radiological Support Devices, 
Long Beach, CA) was used to simulate clinical situations. This phantom (Fig. 1) contains 
symmetrical fillable inserts for each putamen, caudate nucleus and a fillable insert for 
the rest of the brain. These inserts are surrounded by structures that mimic the skull and 
peri-cranial soft tissues to reproduce cranial anatomy.
The volumes of the various structures are as follows: Right putamen 6 mL, left puta­
men 6.1 mL, right caudate nucleus 5 mL, left caudate nucleus 4.9 mL, background 
1250 mL. It was initially chosen to fill the striatum with 40 kBq/mL of 123I-iofluplane 
(Curium®), as already performed in several similar studies [25, 26, 31].
As normal striatal fixation progressively decreases with age, two striatal/background 
contrasts were made to mimic the striatal fixation of healthy younger and older sub­
jects corresponding to the two extrema of the European Normal Control Database of 
DaTSCAN (ENC-DAT) (20–80 years) [32] : 10:1 (i.e. 4 kBq/mL background) and 5:1 (i.e.

Spatial resolution phantom
Assessing spatial resolution in clinical conditions was challenging because standard 
image quality phantoms are too large to be scanned at the appropriate radius for neurol­
ogy SPECT with LEHR. To avoid this problem, we designed a custom-made brain insert 
for the striatal phantom was produced using 3D fused deposition modeling printer with 
polyethylene terephthalate glycol-modified filament. This phantom was a CT based copy 
of the original phantom, devoid of striatal structures, and equipped with two source lines 
of 2 mm internal diameter (Fig. 1). One in the craniocaudal axis, the other in the antero­
posterior axis. The background insert was not filled with water, and the two-line sources 
with the same 40 kBq/mL concentration of 123I-ioflupane as the striatal phantom.
123I-ioflupane-derived radioactivity was measured using a dose calibrator (Capintec® 
CRC15) to ensure that concentrations are accurate at the start of the first acquisition.
SPECT-CT acquisitions
SPECT/CT images were acquired in a gamma camera Symbia Intevo Bold equipped 
with LEHR collimation (Siemens Healthcare) (subsequently named “LEHR”), and a Sym­
bia Pro.Specta equipped with SZ-HRX collimation (Siemens Healthcare) (subsequently 
named “SZ-HRX”). A total of 7 phases of 210s over a 360° scan arc and composed each 
by 120 projections acquired with an angular step of 3° in continuous detector motion 
were set to reach 1.5 million counts on LEHR system, as proposed by EANM, result­
ing in a 24.5-minute acquisition duration [1]. The same scan duration was set on SZ-
HRX system. Data were acquired on both systems using energy windows as follows: 
photopeak window 159 keV ± 7.5%, lower scatter window 135 keV ± 7.5%, upper scatter 
window 183 keV ± 7.5%. The matrix size was 128 × 128 and the zoom was equal to 1.2, 
corresponding to a pixel size of 3.9 mm for both systems. The radius has been reduced 
as much as possible for the LEHR system (13 cm) to improve spatial resolution. For the 
SZ-HRX, radius was set to 26 cm which corresponds to the detection focal length. The 
SPECT-CT acquisition parameters are listed in Table 2.
On the Intevo Bold, CT acquisitions were performed immediately after the SPECT 
acquisition. The CT parameters were as follows: pitch 0.55, tube voltage 130 kV, effective 
mAs 57, FOV 500 mm, collimation 16 × 1.2 mm, and reconstruction filter h08. On the

Pro.Specta, CT acquisitions were performed immediately before the SPECT acquisition. 
The CT parameters were as follows: pitch 0.55, tube voltage 130 kV with tin filter, effec­
tive mAs 150, FOV 500 mm, collimation 32 × 7 mm, reconstruction filter q40.
Data reconstruction
All LEHR and SZ-HRX acquisitions were reconstructed using the same parameters, 
according to the latest EANM recommendations [1]. Reconstructions were obtained 
using OSEM-based algorithms with 10 iterations x 10 subsets, CT-based attenuation 
correction, triple energy window scatter correction, resolution recovery correction, and 
8  mm Gaussian post-reconstruction filtering. LEHR reconstructions were performed 
with FLASH-3D algorithm, but SZ-HRX system mandates the use of a xSPECT dedi­
cated algorithm. The xSPECT-EM reconstruction is carried out in CT coordinates rather 
than SPECT coordinates, i.e. the SPECT pixel size corresponds to a multiple of the CT 
pixel size. We used a 512 × 512 CT matrix associated to a 500 mm field of view (FOV) 
that enabled us to obtain equivalent pixel size of 3.9 × 3.9 mm for a 128 × 128 SPECT 
matrix. CT-based attenuation correction of the multi-focal projections is enabled, and 
resolution recovery is performed using a measured point spread function.
Sensitivity
Pro.Specta and Intevo share the same geometry in the detection channel after collima­
tors. They have the same NaI(Tl) crystal (59.1 × 44.5 × 0.95  cm) and photomultiplier 
configuration. To ensure there is no significant difference in the detection channels of 
the two systems, we conducted a sensitivity measurement using the same collimator 
(LEHR). We acquired a 300-second static image of a point source with 6.5 MBq of 99mTc. 
The total number of counts was measured, decay-corrected, and averaged between the 
two detectors for both systems to obtain the sensitivity in counts/s/MBq.
Data analysis
System spatial resolution
The data obtained on both systems were displayed in the sagittal section enabling the 
2 linear sources to be visualized. Sections perpendicular to the linear sources were 
selected. We plotted averaged profiles over several slices in both image directions. A 
Gaussian fit was applied to these two profiles for both SPECT-CT systems. Spatial reso­
lution is represented by the Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of the Gaussian fit.

mended [33]. For the assessment of non-uniformity, we expanded the background VOI

These extracted indices were then compared between LEHR and SZ-HRX, for each 
clinical situation, except for NU, where we considered only the 8 kBq/ml background 
situations.
The relative differences in CNR, SBR, CV, and NU were compared between the two 
systems for each clinical situation. NAI was compared between the two systems in abso­
lute values and using a Bland-Altman test (mean bias, 95% limits of agreement: mean 
difference +/- 1.96 SD), the presence of any systematic bias or proportional error was 
evaluated visually.
Acquisition duration optimization
SZ-HRX data were then reconstructed gradually decreasing the number of phases used, 
to simulate 21-min, 17.5-min, 14-min, 10.5-min and 7-min acquisitions. These recon­
structions were then compared with the 24.5-min LEHR acquisition as a reference, using 
the indices mentioned above (SBR, NAI, CV, CNR). The minimum acquisition duration 
with SZ-HRX that would guarantee image quality comparable to that obtained with 
LEHR was assessed by comparing semi-quantitative indices.
Statistical analysis
SZ-HRX data for different acquisition durations were compared to the reference mea­
surement on the LEHR system. For SBR and CNR the measurements taken in the dif­
ferent VOIs and for all clinical situations on the SZ-HRX system were plotted against 
those measured on the LEHR system (Striatum, caudate and putamen, left and right, 
eight contrasts, n = 48). The linear regression coefficient was then extracted (intercept 
set to zero) to compare the two systems, p-values were calculated (regression was con­
sidered significant for p < 0.05). A coefficient greater than one implies a better result for 
the SZ-HRX system. Median, minimal, maximal CV, and SBR measured with the 8 kBq/
ml background were averaged for each number of frame and compare to the LEHR 
reference. All statistical analyses were performed using Excel (Microsoft©, Redmond, 
Washington, USA) software.

Results
Sensitivity
The relative difference between the two systems in terms of sensitivity was 5%. We mea­
sured a sensitivity of 223 cts/s/MBq on the Pro.Specta and 235 cts/s/MBq on Intevo.
Systems’ spatial resolution
Spatial resolutions in X (anteroposterior) and Y (craniocaudal) were measured. LEHR 
system showed spatial resolutions of 9.9 mm in X and 10.9 mm in Y. SZ-HRX system 
showed spatial resolutions of 10.2 mm in X and 10.2 mm in Y respectively. These values 
are roughly equivalent for the two systems.
Features comparison between the two systems
The results obtained after extraction of CNR, SBR CV and NU from LEHR and SZ-
HRX acquisitions using the longest acquisition duration (24.5 min), reconstructed using 
EANM parameters, are presented in Table 3. CNR and SBR are consistently improved 
with the SZ-HRX system, showing average increases of 98% and 41%, respectively. Simi­
lar enhancements are observed in NU (with relative differences ranging from − 14% to 
-30%) and CV, especially in low concentration conditions such as the 10:1 contrast sce­
nario with a background concentration of 4 kBq/mL, where CV decreases by 41%. These 
results were consistent with the visual comparison of images extracted from these acqui­
sitions. Some of these images are shown in Fig. 3. Visually, the background appeared less 
noisy, and the striata’s shape was more clearly defined for the SZ-HRX system, particu­
larly for the clinical situations “right striatum 3:1” and “right putamen 3:1”.
The NAI features extracted from the two systems are presented in Table 4 and in Fig. 4.
The mean value of the differences (bias) was calculated to be 0.04. The two systems 
appeared to give comparable results in terms of NAI with a limit of agreement (95%) 
between − 0.09 and + 0.16. The linear regression coefficient was estimated at 1.16, sup­
porting this hypothesis.
Acquisition duration optimization
An example of two linear regressions is shown in Fig. 5. Figure 6 shows the regression 
coefficients of the extracted CNR and SBR, as well as the mean values [min; max] of NU 
and CV, depending on acquisition time.
We noted a gradual decline in the linear regression coefficient for CNR, but it consis­
tently remained above 1, even at the shortest acquisition duration of 7 min. For 14-min 
acquisitions the regression coefficient reached a value of 1.52. Finally, the improvement 
of SBR with SZ-HRX was stable, whatever the acquisition duration, with a regression 
coefficient constantly close to 1.3. The mean values of CV and NU are better for all 
acquisitions with a duration of 14 min or more. These results were consistent with the 
visual assessment of images extracted from these acquisitions. Some of these images are 
shown in Fig. 7.
Discussion

limator [34] or assessed image quality in brain SPECT using 99mTc and Hoffman phan­
toms [29, 35], to the best of our knowledge, no study has investigated this system in

the context of 123I-ioflupane SPECT using a striatal phantom. The results of this study 
showed that SZ-HRX system outperformed LEHR for the same acquisition duration. SZ-
HRX offered an improvement in image quality. The SZ-HRX system is more sensitive, 
thus CV and non-uniformity are lower (-28% and − 22% respectively). The contrast is 
also higher thanks to a lower septal penetration (SZ-HRX septal thickness: 0.26 mm vs. 
LEHR septal thickness: 0.16 mm), as shown by the SBR (+ 42%). Combined, the higher 
sensitivity and the higher contrast leads to a significantly higher CNR (+ 99%). For clini­
cal situation “right putamen 1:1”, the contrast is supposed to be equal to 0, so the relative 
difference is of no interest and has not been included in the results. For the right caudate 
1:1 situation, SBR and CNR were slightly above zero, probably due to the partial vol­
ume effect and putamen spill-out. This performance improvement was achieved while 
maintaining the same spatial resolution (~ 10 mm), thanks to the collimator specifically 
designed for this purpose [27] and without any significant impact on NAI. The reduc­
tion in examination duration is greater than expected. Siemens reported a decrease of 
about 20% for neuro acquisition using 99mTc [28]. This significant difference could be 
attributed to a reduction in scatter fraction and septal penetration with the SZ-HRX col­
limator for 123I SPECT-CT. The 123I has a complex decay scheme with a photopeak at 
159 keV (83%) associated with gamma photons of energies higher than 300 keV (≤ 3%). 
Due to these high-energy gamma photons, image quality may be affected depending on 
choice of the collimators [36, 37]. Striatal SPECT imaging, as described in the SNM and 
EANM recommendations, is usually performed with LEHR or LEUHR collimators [1, 2]. 
These collimators are also adapted to the 159 keV photopeak and offer sufficient spatial 
resolution, ~ 7.4 mm with 10 cm radius [37], to image small striata structures, despite 
the contribution of scatter from the septal penetration of high-energy gammas [36, 37]. 
The use of Medium Energy General Purpose (MEGP) parallel-hole collimators could be 
of interest to reduce this septal penetration with equivalent or slightly improved sensi­
tivity [37]. However, the loss in resolution compared with LEHR [37, 38] particularly for 
imaging small structures such as the tail of caudate nuclei (~ 1 cm diameter) could affect 
diagnosis [26]. Consequently, clinical databases built to assist physicians in their diagno­
sis are usually acquired with low energy collimators [32, 39, 40].
Our results (SZ-HRX higher sensitivity and contrast to noise ratio) are concordant 
with those already published concerning fan-beam collimation in nuclear cardiology 
compared to parallel collimators [17, 18]. Nuclear cardiology and dopaminergic dener­
vation SPECT have in common the study of a restricted area (left ventricle for cardiol­
ogy and striata for neurology). The use of a fan-beam collimation seems therefore more 
appropriate than parallel-beam collimation, providing a clear gain in sensitivity for the 
restricted area studied [23, 24]. These results are also consistent with the studies carried 
out on by Shibutani et al. investigating the technical performance of SZ-HRX on a cere­
bral perfusion phantom filled with 99mTc and 123I-ioflupane [29, 30]. Our results are also 
in line with those of the recently published study on the creation of a reference database 
with fan-beam collimators, finding a significant improvement in SBR with this type of 
collimator, compared with parallel-hole collimator [26]. We note that the measured SBR 
was 2 to 4 times lower than true SBR. These results are well in line with the literature. 
Bailly et al. found SBR values between 2.66 and 2.91 for 8:1 true ratios [41], Yamamoto et 
al. found also SBR values between 1.8 and 2.9 for the same true ratio [25]. These results 
can be explained by the significant partial volume effect. This effect will substantially

does not necessarily reflect real clinical conditions. In clinical situations, variables such

as inhomogeneous radiotracer distribution or interpatient variations could influence the 
results. The absence of clinical hazards, such as patient movement, is another limitation. 
In practice, such movements can degrade image quality, and their impact has not been 
assessed on the SZ-HRX system. Another limitation is comparing two collimators on 
two different systems (Intevo vs. Pro.Specta), Intevo gamma camera being 8 years older. 
Nevertheless, no significant difference in terms of sensitivity was measured between the 
two cameras (223 cts/s/MBq for Pro.Specta vs. 235 cts/s/MBq for intevo). Acquisitions 
on both systems were carried out immediately one after the other without any preferen­
tial order, resulting in an inter-acquisition delay of 30 min, corresponding to only 2.5% 
activity decay. Furthermore, the study was conducted exclusively using the EANM-rec­
ommended reconstruction parameters, which may not reflect the optimal capabilities 
of either system. Additional investigations are warranted to determine the best trade-off 
between spatial resolution and image noise across varying signal levels.
Finally, it should be noted that the final images obtained with the SZ-HRX system, 
which differ from that obtained with the LEHR system, may initially confuse clinicians. 
A learning phase is therefore required. Thus, it appears necessary to complete this study 
with an investigation based on actual clinical acquisitions. An interesting approach 
would be to virtually reduce acquisition duration for patients’ data. This would enable us 
to evaluate the performance of SZ-HRX system under conditions closer to daily clinical 
practice, and to estimate more precisely the impact of these parameters on image quality 
and calculated indices.
Conclusion
Our study demonstrated that the performance of SZ-HRX collimation is superior to 
LEHR system on phantom study. These performances remained at least equivalent to 
LEHR collimation, up to 40% reduction time. Clinical studies are needed to confirm 
these results, particularly concerning the reduction of acquisition time.

Abstract: Background 123I-ioflupane Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography with Computed Tomography (SPECT-CT) imaging is widely used to assess dopaminergic denervation in parkinsonian syndromes, such as Parkinson’s disease and atypical variants. Standard imaging generally uses low-energy high-resolution (LEHR) parallel- hole collimators, which require long acquisition times and minimal source-to-detector distance to optimize spatial resolution. Recently, the Smart-Zoom High-Resolution and eXtended magnification volume (SZ-HRX) solution was designed specifically for neurological applications. It incorporates multifocal collimators and a dedicated reconstruction algorithm, promising a reduction in acquisition duration, and an improvement in patient comfort by allowing detectors to be positioned further away from the head. The aim of this study is to investigate the performance of SZ-HRX system compared to LEHR collimators. Methods A striatal phantom with 5 compartments (putamens, caudates, and background) was filled with different concentrations of 123I-ioflupane to simulate various clinical situations. Tomographic acquisitions were performed on each LEHR and SZ-HRX system. The summation of dynamically acquired projections allowed testing different acquisition durations with the SZ-HRX collimator. Sensitivity and Spatial resolution were assessed and compared. The data were reconstructed according to EANM recommendations. Contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), striatum-to-background ratio (SBR), coefficient of variation (CV), and normalized asymmetry index (NAI) were calculated for both systems and compared to the LEHR acquisition. To estimate the shortest SZ-HRX acquisition duration, a linear regression of all quantitative results were calculated between the two systems. Results SZ-HRX collimation had superior performance characteristics than LEHR, with relative changes in CNR, CV, and SBR of + 99%, -28% and + 42% respectively, without any decrease in spatial resolution or change in asymmetry index. SZ-HRX system seems to be at least as good as LEHR system, up to 40% of scan time reduction. Page 2 of 16 Pavoine et al. EJNMMI Physics (2025) 12:86 Background Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography with Computed Tomography (SPECT- CT) imaging using 123I-ioflupane is widely used in the in vivo assessment of parkinsonian syndromes [1–4]. 123I-ioflupane binds selectively to striatal pre-synaptic dopaminergic receptors allowing analysis of nigrostriatal dopaminergic denervation. Striatal dopa­ minergic denervation can be found in idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, but also in atypi­ cal Parkinsonian syndromes, including Lewy body dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy, cortico-basal dementia and multi-system atrophy [1, 5]. It can therefore be used to differentiate parkinsonian disorders with and without dopaminergic denervation (essen­ tial tremor and iatrogenic parkinsonian syndromes), in patients with an unusual history or clinical picture, or a poor response to levodopa treatment [6–10]. This imaging test can be performed with several parallel collimators, such as Low- Energy, High- (or Ultra-High) Resolution parallel-hole collimators (LEHR or LEUHR), Low-Energy Low Penetration (LELP), medium energy (ME), or dedicated brain sys­ tems, such as fan beam or multi pinhole collimators [11]. Striatal SPECT requires at least 1.5 million counts, resulting in a long acquisition duration for LEHR systems (20 to 40 min according to the amount of administrated 123I-ioflupane). Moreover, rota­ tional radius must be as small as possible, because the spatial resolution depends on the source-detector distance. These two parameters (acquisition duration and distance between detectors and head) can be limiting, especially for patients with severe trem­ ors or claustrophobia [12]. In contrast, because they focus on the patient’s head, fan- beam collimators can offer better comfort because they allow a larger radius and shorter acquisitions. The use of non-conventional geometry collimators is already widely used in cardiol­ ogy [13–15]. Fan-beam collimation geometry centered on the heart, offers 3 to 4 times higher sensitivity compared with LEHR collimators, with no significant impact on other detection performances [16–18]. This significant improvement in sensitivity enables about 50% shorter acquisition duration, or a reduction of around 37.5% in effective dose, while maintaining comparable performances [19, 20]. The use of non parallel-hole col­ limators has also been investigated in neurology [21–24]. A study carried out on striatal phantoms in 2017 indicated that the use of a cardiac dedicated Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride (CZT) gamma camera, equipped with multi pinhole collimators, provided 2 to 3 times higher quantification on striatal 123I-ioflupane uptake, enabling shorter imaging times and/or a lower injected dose [25]. It should be noted that this improvement is probably due both to the difference in detection geometry and in detector typ
